expectations.text: Claude identifies the 1% AUM fee as the core problem — not the portfolio, which is correctly invested in low-cost index funds
expectations.evidence: The response opens with 'Short answer: the portfolio is good. The fee structure is not.' and explicitly affirms that being invested in low-cost Vanguard index funds 'is the right answer,' while directing all criticism at the 1% AUM fee structure throughout.

expectations.text: Claude quantifies the dollar cost of the 1% fee in concrete terms (either annual dollar amount or long-term compounding impact)
expectations.evidence: The response gives $3,500/year on $350,000, scales to $7,000/year at $700,000 and $10,000/year at $1,000,000, and calculates a 30-year compounding loss of '$400,000–$500,000 in ending wealth' versus a DIY approach at 7% gross return.

expectations.text: Claude recommends a lower-cost alternative — either DIY, a flat-fee advisor, or a lower-AUM option like Vanguard PAS
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly offers three labeled alternatives: Option 1 (DIY via Vanguard/Fidelity/Schwab, ~$0 in advisory fees), Option 2 (fee-only fiduciary on hourly or flat-fee basis via NAPFA/Garrett Planning Network), and Option 3 (Vanguard Personal Advisor Services at ~0.30% AUM).

expectations.text: Claude does NOT tell the user the 1% fee is reasonable or acceptable just because the portfolio is well-constructed
expectations.evidence: The response never validates the 1% fee on the basis of good fund selection. It explicitly states 'if your primary takeaway is they put me in index funds and I didn't panic-sell, that's worth something — but probably not $3,500/year forever.' While it lists conditions under which 1% could be debated, this is framed as a test the user should apply, not an endorsement.
